feed.title: Combined summary - Handling PQ signatures on the stack

entry.title: Combined summary - Handling PQ signatures on the stack
entry.summary: Enabling post-quantum (PQ) signature support in Bitcoin Script is essential for future-proofing the protocol against threats posed by quantum computing. Most practical PQ signature schemes require larger data sizes than currently supported, prompting a proposal to increase the stack element size in TapScript from 520 bytes to 6 kilobytes, as outlined in [this BIP draft](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76). This upgrade aims to facilitate the integration of robust cryptographic mechanisms like those developed by the SHRINCS initiative. However, such an increase introduces heightened risks of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, since certain opcodes can be exploited to consume excessive computational resources when operating on large stack elements. The threat primarily arises from opcodes that duplicate or hash stack elements, especially those without hardware acceleration (e.g., `OP_RIPEMD160`) or those that process data byte-by-byte (`OP_VERIFY`, `OP_IFDUP`, `OP_EQUAL`). If attackers can repeatedly manipulate large elements, they could significantly amplify CPU usage, undermining network stability. These concerns necessitate both protocol-level and implementation-specific countermeasures to ensure that expanded script capabilities do not compromise security or performance. Several strategies have been considered to address these challenges. One conservative method involves maintaining the existing 520-byte consensus limit and requiring chunked processing for larger items. While this approach minimizes immediate changes to consensus rules, it complicates wallet and script development due to cumbersome encoding and parsing requirements across multiple chunks. Another strategy suggests blacklisting specific opcodes—such as limiting duplication operations—to prevent repeated manipulation of large data, thus mitigating DoS vectors. Although effective for resource control, this method restricts the range of possible script innovations, especially those involving advanced manipulations of signature data. A more comprehensive approach advocates for optimizing opcode implementations so that their resource consumption scales efficiently with input size. Techniques such as representing stack elements as pointers, introducing hash-caching, and optimizing truthiness checks can reduce computational overhead without altering consensus rules. These improvements would enhance performance but place significant demands on node software development and carry the risk of unforeseen vulnerabilities if edge cases are overlooked. Another ambitious solution draws inspiration from [BIP-440](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/9f3d3bc6a60db16efbdc71ac8f7ea30217fc0c39/bip-0440.mediawiki), proposing the adoption of a formal computational budget system—varops—that enforces transaction-level limits on compute and memory usage. Such a system would allow scripts to handle large data and complex logic while maintaining strict controls over resource allocation, directly addressing DoS risks but at the cost of increased protocol complexity and the need for extensive testing. Isolating signature operations onto a dedicated "sigstack" offers a streamlined alternative. In this model, only signature-checking opcodes interact with large signature data, limiting the exposure of general script logic to potential exploitation. While this reduces flexibility by precluding creative uses of signature data within scripts, it simplifies implementation and opens the possibility of offering greater transaction fee discounts, as discussed in [this forum topic](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/segwit-commitment-to-post-quantum-witness-data/2702). Each proposed path involves trade-offs between security, utility, simplicity, and compatibility. Avoiding arbitrary limitations aligns with TapScript's philosophy of upgradable limits, which supports future enhancements without legacy baggage. Imposing artificial restrictions, such as mandatory chunking or opcode blacklisting, is seen as counterproductive, as it stifles innovation and may inadvertently restrict valuable new functionalities. Relying solely on implementation optimizations risks missing edge cases, potentially compromising security and creating maintenance burdens. A hybrid approach that combines selective opcode restrictions with implementation optimizations appears promising, balancing performance with safety. For example, pointer-based stack representations could render some operations constant-time, while high-cost opcodes might be explicitly restricted for large stack elements. However, any such scheme must be designed carefully to avoid precluding legitimate use cases or introducing new attack surfaces. In summary, supporting PQ signatures in Bitcoin Script requires a nuanced balance: increasing script capacity to accommodate new cryptographic primitives while safeguarding network robustness and developer usability. Solutions range from minimal adjustments that maintain backward compatibility to sweeping protocol reforms that enable sophisticated functionality with strong resource controls. Ongoing community engagement and rigorous technical analysis will be vital as the ecosystem moves toward integrating PQ cryptography into Bitcoin’s scripting language.
